OnePlus and the Amazon title both describe the Watch 3 as Android-only, while Smartprix's spec sheet claims iOS support — worth settling before an iPhone owner buys one. OnePlus publishes no peak brightness figure for that watch at all. And the Huawei Watch GT 6 is not sold in the US; the price shown is a conversion of its roughly 260 euro European price, for comparison only.

intro: The wattage on a multi-port charger is what one port delivers on its own, and the protocol behind it decides whether your particular phone or laptop can use it. Both are recorded per port here rather than as a single headline figure.

traps.title: The wattage on the box is a single-port figure
traps.body: UGREEN's Nexode 65W drops to 45W plus 8.5W plus 8.5W once all three ports are occupied, so it cannot fast-charge a laptop and a phone at the same time. Belkin's 45W dual becomes 25W plus 20W with both ports in use. Anker's Prime 100W gives 65W plus 35W across two USB-C, and 89W total across three. The Baseus PicoGo 140W splits to 70W plus 70W, or 90W plus 45W. INIU publishes no per-port table at all, and neither does UGREEN for the Nexode X 160W.

traps.title: Without PPS, a 65W charger charges a Galaxy at 25W
traps.body: Samsung's 45W Super Fast Charging 2.0 and several other fast-charge modes require PPS (Programmable Power Supply), not just USB-C PD. Samsung's own 45W publishes the range that triggers it: 3.3-21V/2.25A. Apple's 20W has PD 2.0 and 3.0 with no PPS at all, and Apple's 40W Dynamic uses AVS rather than PPS, so it will not trigger Samsung's mode either. Anker's Nano 30W and UGREEN's Nexode 30W both carry PPS and publish their windows.

traps.title: A USB-A port will not fast-charge a modern iPhone or MacBook
traps.body: USB-A tops out at Quick Charge speeds no matter what the charger's total rating says, and the per-port numbers show it: the Anker Prime 67W and Prime 100W both give 22.5W from USB-A against 67W and 100W from USB-C, and the Baseus PicoGo 140W gives 44W from USB-A against 140W from C1 or C2. Count the USB-C ports rather than the total — the UGREEN Nexode 65W's three ports are two USB-C and one USB-A.

traps.title: GaN affects size and heat, not charging speed
traps.body: Marketing tends to imply otherwise, but speed is set by wattage and protocol; GaN shows up in the dimensions and the weight, which is where it is worth comparing. Samsung names the part in its 45W (GaN Systems GS-065-008-1-L), Anker brands its version GaNPrime and UGREEN calls its own GaNInfinity. Apple's 20W is not GaN at all, and Apple does not state the switching material for the 40W Dynamic — teardowns have not confirmed it either.

intro: In this category the spec sheet and the marketing disagree more often than they agree: "2K" and "4K" are pixel totals rather than widths, the wired models split over transformer voltage, and several of these doorbells record nothing at all until you start paying monthly.

traps.title: Several of these record nothing at all without a monthly plan
traps.body: With no subscription a Ring doorbell — including the $249.99 Battery Doorbell Pro 4K — records nothing and fires no person or package alerts; it is a live-view intercom. Tom's Guide describes the unsubscribed Arlo as "stripped to a grossly basic live view and motion detector functionality", and Arlo Secure has risen from $2.99 to $4.99 to $7.99 a month for one camera. SimpliSafe's cheapest recording plan is $9.99/mo. Google is the outlier among cloud brands: person, package, vehicle and animal alerts plus six hours of event previews cost nothing.

traps.title: "2K" and "4K" here count total pixels, not the width of the frame
traps.body: Every doorbell here that shoots a square frame counts total pixels. Ring's "Retinal 2K" is 1920 x 1920 and Blink's $39.99 "2K+" is the identical 1920 x 1920, for which Ring charges $99.99. Ring's "Retinal 4K" is 2880 x 2880, 960 pixels narrower than UHD; Arlo's 2K is 1944 x 1944 and Wyze's is 2048 x 1536. The genuinely sharper sensors are cheaper: Reolink and Tapo both shoot a real 5MP 2560 x 1920 and the Lorex is 8MP. Google publishes no pixel count for the Nest's "2K HDR" at all.

traps.title: Older doorbell transformers rule out the Nest, the Wyze and the Lorex
traps.body: Wired models split into two camps and the split is invisible in marketing. Google's Nest demands 16-24VAC at 10-40VA, Wyze 16-24VAC at 10VA or more, and the Lorex 16-24VAC — none runs on the 8-10VAC transformer common in older US houses. Ring accepts 8-24VAC, SimpliSafe 8-24VAC at 30VA max, and Blink, Aqara and Reolink take 12-24VAC; Reolink ships an indoor plug-in adapter, so it needs no transformer at all. Blink's FAQ adds that its Wired Doorbell 2K+ "does not ring your existing in-home mechanical chime" without a bypass cable that disables it, and SimpliSafe supports mechanical chimes only.

traps.title: A 16:9 frame shows the visitor's face but not the parcel on the mat
traps.body: A 1:1 or 3:4 frame shows a visitor head-to-toe plus the doormat; 16:9 and 4:3 do not. SimpliSafe sells a 16:9 1080p camera for $169, and Wyze is 4:3 at 135° horizontal. Reolink is the strangest case: the same product name ships 4:3 in black and 3:4 in white, so the colour you pick changes the framing. eufy sidesteps the problem with a second downward-facing lens. Google's own page says 1:1 while Tom's Guide's review says 3:4, and Aqara lists a 4:3 ratio beside a 16:9 sensor output on one page.

traps.title: "Local storage" usually means buying a hub that isn't in the box
traps.body: Aqara, Reolink, Wyze, Lorex and Tapo record to a card you control — Lorex ships one fitted, and Tapo's card goes in the included hub. eufy is the only one with storage inside the doorbell itself, 8GB of eMMC, expandable only by adding a HomeBase S280 or S380 sold separately. Blink needs a Sync Module 2 or Sync Module XR, neither of which is in the $39.99 box, and Arlo needs a SmartHub or Base Station. Ring, Nest and SimpliSafe have no local storage path at any price.

traps.title: Battery claims here come without the events-per-day they assume
traps.body: Ring publishes no runtime figure at all for either of its battery doorbells. Arlo claims "up to 6 months, dependent on usage" and Aqara five months on six AA cells, neither with an event count; eufy publishes nothing, though Linkd Home's 30-day heavy-use test projected roughly 78 days. SafeWise's tester recharged the $249.99 Ring 4K Pro about every two weeks on a busy porch while Tom's Guide lost under 25% in a fortnight on a quiet one. Only TP-Link states its assumption: 180 days at 10-20 events a day.

traps.title: Only five of these twelve have a 5GHz radio
traps.body: The Ring Battery Doorbell Pro 4K (Wi-Fi 6, and it wants 15 Mbps upload), the Nest 3rd gen (802.11ac), the Aqara G410, the Reolink and the Lorex are the five with a 5GHz radio. The $99.99 Ring Battery Doorbell 2K is single-band Wi-Fi 4 while its own $249.99 stablemate is dual-band Wi-Fi 6. Arlo, eufy, Wyze, Blink, SimpliSafe and Tapo are 2.4GHz only, which matters if your router hands out a single combined network.

traps.title: A Matter badge on a doorbell has nothing to do with its video
traps.body: Matter carries no camera stream, so the badge refers to something else. The Aqara G410 is the only Matter device here, and its Matter role is as a controller and Thread border router for other people's gear; its own video reaches Apple Home through HomeKit Secure Video, which downgrades the stream — Aqara states "when using the HSV, the maximum resolution is 1200p". Real Apple Home support in this set is Aqara and Arlo, whose community manager confirmed it for 2nd-gen devices in March 2025.

intro: This is the category with the most misleading marketing on the site. "MagSafe compatible" is a claim about magnets, "up to 25W" is a claim about somebody else's phone, and half of these arrive without the brick they need to hit their rated speed.

traps.title: "MagSafe compatible" describes the magnets, not the charging speed
traps.body: A pad can align perfectly and still be plain Qi at 7.5W. The $22.99 ESR HaloLock kickstand is exactly that: one third the speed of the Qi2.2 pads that cost $10 to $20 more, despite the "MagSafe compatible" marketing. Qi2 means 15W with Wireless Power Consortium certification and Qi2.2 means 25W; the Qi standard row on each page states which certification a charger actually holds, or that it holds neither.

traps.title: Six of these twelve ship without a power adapter
traps.body: The Anker MagGo pad, UGREEN MagFlow pad, ESR HaloLock kickstand, Apple's 25W MagSafe, the UGREEN MagFlow 2-in-1 and the Twelve South Butterfly SE all arrive without one. Several also need a specific PD wattage to reach their rated speed — 30W or better for the 15W pads, 45W for UGREEN's 2-in-1 — so that is a real $20 to $40 addition to the price. Belkin's UltraCharge is sold as two listings differing only by whether an adapter is included, roughly $10 to $15 apart.

traps.title: "Up to 25W" is a claim about the phone, not the charger
traps.body: Qi2.2's 25W applies only to phones that support Qi2.2. iPhone 12 through 15 fall back to 15W on the UGREEN MagFlow, the Belkin UltraCharge and the other 25W pads, and many Android handsets fall back to 5W or to the maker's own proprietary rate. Apple's 2025 MagSafe revision is Qi2 25W certified, so it does reach 25W on Pixel and other Qi2.2 phones as well as iPhone. Check your handset against the max phone watts row.

traps.title: Belkin's "2-in-1" is phone plus AirPods, not phone plus watch
traps.body: That is a very common misreading, and the AirPods port on it is only 5W. The Twelve South Butterfly SE charges a phone plus an Apple Watch, or AirPods on the watch puck, but not both at once. Multi-device stands also share one supply exactly as wired chargers do, so a 3-in-1 rarely delivers its phone-pad maximum while a watch and earbuds are drawing from it too. Read the devices-charged row before assuming a count.

traps.title: Only two of these hold 25W under sustained load
traps.body: The ESR CryoBoost 3-in-1 uses an active fan and the Anker Prime 3-in-1 pairs active cooling with a folding body; both sustain 25W rather than throttling. The Satechi 3-in-1 and the Baseus PicoGo 3-in-1 are passively cooled and will drop below 25W under sustained load. That is the difference between a rated figure and a delivered one, and the cooling row on each page says which you are buying.

traps.title: The superseded 2024 MagSafe is still on sale at nearly the same price
traps.body: Apple's 2024 puck sits alongside the 2025 revision on Amazon at a nearly identical price, and it is not Qi2 25W certified — the listing title is the only thing separating them. Anker's own product page for the Prime 3-in-1 says a 45W adapter is needed separately, while the Amazon listing and reviews confirm one is included. Both conflicts are shown here rather than quietly resolved, so check the title and in-box contents before ordering.

traps.title: Past roughly 3mm of case, alignment and charge rate both fall off
traps.body: Magnetic alignment and charging speed degrade beyond about 3mm of case thickness, so a thick wallet case, a battery case or a ring accessory can pull a genuinely certified Qi2 pad below its rated speed or stop it holding the phone at all. Each product page records the manufacturer's own stated case limit, which is worth reading against the case you actually use rather than a bare phone.
